Basic Accounting Concepts

This pre-term module is designed to provide a solid foundation in accounting before your MBA begins. It covers fundamental accounting concepts through video courses, quick reference materials, practice quizzes, and an optional book for deeper understanding.

Fact: “Every financial transaction in a business tells a story. Understanding accounting helps you read and write that story effectively.”

Here is a video showcasing how accounting impacts business decisions and financial stability.

Why Accounting Matters 

Objectives

By the end of this module, you’ll be able to:

Understand key accounting principles such as accrual vs. cash accounting.

Read and interpret financial statements (Income Statement, Balance Sheet, and Cash Flow Statement).

Record basic journal entries for transactions.

Apply fundamental accounting concepts to real-world business scenarios.

Basics of Accounting and Setting Up Company


“Every financial transaction in a business tells a story. Understanding accounting helps you read and write that story effectively.”


1. The 3 Financial Statements


Every business, no matter the size, relies on three core financial statements to understand what’s happening inside the company and make informed decisions. A strong CEO stays on top of every number, understands what’s driving them, and uses them to guide strategy, spending, and growth.

Statement

What it shows

Why it matters

Key questions it answers

Income Statement (P&L)

Profit or loss over a period

Tracks whether you’re making or burning money

Are we profitable? Where are we spending the most?

Balance Sheet

What you own vs what you owe

Shows financial health at a point in time

Do we have enough to survive? How much do we owe?

Cash Flow Statement

Actual cash in and out

Determines survival

Will we run out of cash? When do we need funding?

 

2. What do these statements look like and how do we read them?


Income Statement (P&L)

Item

Amount (₹)

Explanation

Revenue

50,000

Money earned from selling your core product/service

Other Income

+5,000

(Income not from core business - e.g., grants, prize money, cashback)

Total Income

55,000

Revenue + Other Income

COGS (Cost of Goods Sold)

-20,000

Direct cost to produce product/service (materials, delivery, etc.)

Gross Profit

35,000

Total Income − COGS

Direct Expenses (Payment gateway fees, discounts, Platform commissions)

-5000

Pure variable, directly linked-to-each-sale costs, the ones that increase every time you sell one more unit.

CM1 (Contribution Margin 1)

30,000

(Revenue - Direct variable costs + COGS; shows unit-level profitability)

Operating Expenses (Variable)

-10,000

Marketing, commissions, delivery (changes with sales)

CM2 (Contribution Margin 2)

20,000

(CM1 - variable operating costs; shows how much is left to cover fixed costs)

Operating Expenses (Fixed)

-8,000

Salaries, rent, software (doesn’t change with sales)

EBITDA

12,000

Profit before interest, tax, depreciation

Interest on Loan

-1000

Any interest paid on loan

Depreciation

-500

Any depreciation incurred on fixed assets (good to claim expenses if tax reduction is the goal and not inflated profit)

Tax Paid

-500

 

Net Profit

10,000

Final profit after all expenses


It helps you answer questions around income, expense & profitability, for eg:

Is our revenue actually growing - and at what pace (2x, 3x, flat)?
Which costs are hurting us the most (ads, salaries, tech)?
Are we moving towards profitability or drifting away from it?
CM1 → Are we making money per unit sold?
CM2 → Is the business viable before fixed costs?

A common mistake is celebrating revenue without understanding how expensive that growth is.

40,000

(Asset = Liabilities + Equity) (Usually prepared at end of the financial year, ie 31st March or quarterly for analysis)

It helps you answer:
How much cash do we actually have in the bank today?
How much do we owe (vendors, loans, liabilities)?
How much of the company is funded by founders vs investors?
How much inventory do we hold, and how much cash is stuck in it?

Cash Flow Statement

(Start with the cash you have, add everything you receive, subtract everything you spend - what’s left is your closing cash.)

It helps you answer:
Are we burning more cash than we’re bringing in?
How many months of runway do we have?
Are we dependent on funding to stay alive?

A startup can look profitable on paper and still shut down because it runs out of cash

5. GST 


GST (Goods and Services Tax) is a tax you collect from your customer on behalf of the government.

It is not your income - you are simply passing it through.

The Flow 


You sell → you charge GST → Output GST
You buy → you pay GST → Input GST
You pay the difference to the government

Example

You sell for ₹1,000 + ₹180 GST
You paid ₹80 GST on expenses

You pay the government:
₹180 − ₹80 = ₹100

6. Why Startup Accounting Matters


Most founders delay accounting and regret it later.

Starting early helps because:

You can claim losses later
Early-stage losses can reduce future tax when you become profitable

Fundraising becomes easier
Clean numbers build investor trust quickly

You make better decisions
You know where money is going and what’s working

You avoid chaos later
Fixing bad accounting is painful, expensive, and risky
